name: Authorization Best Practices
description: This module captures the best practices for authorization, distilled from common failure modes and what tends to hold up over time.
content:
This module captures the best practices for authorization, distilled from common failure modes and what tends to hold up over time.

CORE GUIDELINES
1. Keep authorization outputs reproducible: fix seeds, record versions, and avoid hidden non-determinism where it matters.
2. Document any non-obvious authorization decision with a short rationale so future readers understand the 'why', not just the 'what'.
3. Prefer the simplest authorization approach that satisfies the requirement over a more general one that isn't needed yet.
4. When authorization guidance conflicts with a specific user instruction, defer to the user's explicit instruction and note the conflict.
5. Prefer explicit, readable authorization solutions over clever ones that are hard to verify.
6. Surface known limitations of a chosen authorization approach instead of presenting it as complete when it is not.
7. When authorization decisions are ambiguous, favor the option that is easiest to reverse or extend later.
8. Validate authorization outputs against a concrete example before treating the work as complete.
9. When multiple authorization strategies are viable, name the trade-off explicitly rather than silently picking one.
10. Before starting authorization work, confirm the scope and constraints so the approach matches the actual requirement.
11. Keep authorization changes scoped to what was asked; avoid unrelated cleanup in the same pass.

COMMON PITFALLS TO AVOID
- Do not apply generic authorization advice without checking it fits the specific context at hand.
- Do not skip documenting authorization assumptions just because they seem obvious in the moment.
- Do not silently drop authorization edge cases to make an example look cleaner than the real system.
- Avoid mixing unrelated authorization concerns into a single change; keep each change focused.

CLOSING NOTE
These guidelines are a starting point for authorization, not an exhaustive rulebook — use judgment when a rule doesn't fit the situation.
